evidence.title: Medical Student Experiences With ChatGPT: National Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.outcome: Association between baseline AI understanding and cross-checking or editing of ChatGPT output

evidence.quote: Students who reported moderate or advanced baseline understanding of AI were more likely to practice conscientious use habits, such as cross-checking (odds ratio [OR] 2.31, 95% CI 1.08-4.97) and editing (OR 2.45, 95% CI 1.05-5.71) ChatGPT output before using it, than those who reported a basic or limited understanding.

evidence.outcome: GP knowledge gaps about AI as an adoption barrier and need for further AI training
evidence.effect: Lack of knowledge about suitable AI applications and how AI works was the biggest barrier; 83 of 149 (55.7%) GPs expressed a need for further AI training.
evidence.quote: The biggest barrier to AI implementation was a lack of knowledge about suitable AI-based applications and of how AI works.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence in Military Graduate Medical Education: Trainee Perceptions and Current Use
evidence.outcome: Trainee AI literacy training gap and desire for formal AI education
evidence.effect: 84% agreed a need for formal AI training exists; 73% disagreed that their current curriculum contained enough; only 10 had prior formal AI training.
evidence.quote: Eighty-four percent of trainees agreed with a need for formal AI training, while 73% disagreed that their current curriculum contained enough.

evidence.title: Pediatric nurses' use of generative artificial intelligence and their competency levels
evidence.outcome: Proportion of pediatric nurses with AI training and self-perceived competence using generative AI
evidence.effect: Only 9.3% (n = 51) had received AI training; 77.2% (n = 27) of generative AI users did not feel competent; mean scale score 48.97 ± 10.07.
evidence.quote: It was determined that very few nurses had received training related to artificial intelligence (9.3%, n = 51), used generative artificial intelligence applications, and that the majority of those who used them (77.2%, n = 27) did not feel competent while using the applications.

evidence.title: ICU Nurses' Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence in Adult Intensive Care Units: Knowledge, Attitudes and Job-Security Concerns
evidence.outcome: ICU nurses' knowledge of AI concepts (survey score)
evidence.effect: AI knowledge ranged from limited to moderate (mean 4.18 ± 1.50); greater knowledge was associated with more positive attitudes (r = 0.366) and lower job security concerns (r = -0.302).
evidence.quote: AI knowledge ranged from limited to moderate (mean 4.18 ± 1.50).

evidence.title: [The use of artificial intelligence tools in the perception of electroradiologists]
evidence.outcome: Electroradiologists' AI knowledge and training adequacy
evidence.effect: Most respondents know the general concept of AI but lack detailed knowledge. Insufficient education and a need for training were reported. Lack of training limits readiness for implementation.
evidence.quote: Despite a positive attitude towards AI, a lack of training limits readiness for its implementation.

evidence.title: Knowledge and Use of Artificial Intelligence Among Oncology Faculty and Trainees at a Comprehensive Cancer Center in 2025
evidence.outcome: Staff need for AI training and knowledge of learning resources
evidence.effect: Nearly 93% of respondents endorsed the need for dedicated AI training, and approximately half reported not knowing where to find reliable learning resources.
evidence.quote: Nearly 93% of respondents endorsed the need for dedicated AI training, and approximately half reported not knowing where to find reliable learning resources.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence and ChatGPT literacy among surgical healthcare professionals: knowledge, attitudes, and perceived clinical utility
evidence.outcome: Proportion of surgical trainees and specialists with formal AI training and AI/ChatGPT literacy
evidence.effect: 93.2% of participants lacked formal AI training; 80.9% had prior ChatGPT experience; consultants reported lower familiarity than trainees; lack of training was a reported barrier.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence in health systems of the WHO European region: implementation, applications, opportunities, and barriers
evidence.outcome: Member States offering AI training to the health workforce (in-service and pre-service)
evidence.effect: Only 24% (12/50) of Member States offered in-service AI training for the health workforce, and 20% (10/50) offered pre-service training.
evidence.quote: Finally, with regard to health workforce education and AI literacy, the study highlights a significant gap in preparedness, where only 24% of Member States (12/50) reported offering in-service AI training for the health workforce, and 20% (10/50) offered pre-service training.

evidence.title: Current Landscape of Generative AI Use as a Search Engine Among Resident Physicians: Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.outcome: Resident physicians' GenAI literacy, including understanding of confabulation and ethical considerations

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence in rheumatology and paediatric rheumatology: insights from an international survey by EMEUNET

evidence.title: Perceptions, knowledge and adoption of artificial intelligence in rheumatology: results from a British Society for Rheumatology survey

commentary.bottom_line: Thirteen studies suggest that AI education is associated with higher self-reported knowledge, self-efficacy, trust, and cross-checking of AI output, but most are small, uncontrolled, or cross-sectional, and four found null or mixed results. No study linked staff AI literacy education to fewer errors or to patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Two simulated randomized trials found that basic information raised staff trust in decision support by 5% and lowered distrust by 3 to 4% (n=780), and that an intervention improved nurses' ethical awareness (n=46). The other eleven are single-group or cross-sectional self-report studies. Three found no significant gain in literacy or knowledge, and one found none in intention to use AI.

Among 102 and 177 medical students, those with more AI understanding were more likely to cross-check LLM output (5.06 times; OR 2.31) and to edit it (OR 2.45). Literacy may therefore support checking behavior. These are observational associations in students, and no study measured whether errors were caught before reaching patients.

A 30-minute presentation did not significantly raise intention to use AI. A one-day workshop raised self-rated skills, and an 8-week hospital program produced self-efficacy gains (d=1.57) while job-specific competency stayed below the scale midpoint. Short programs may raise confidence faster than practical skill.

No test of the practice enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A qualitative study of five U.S. safety-net organizations found gaps in foundational AI education and a lack of training resources. That study shows the need exists in these settings but does not show that education programs work there.

In a UK survey of 409 medical physics and engineering staff, 10% had prior AI education and 23% knew where to find training, and preparedness rose about threefold with education. Across 50 WHO European Member States, 24% offered in-service AI training. No study reported program cost or staff time required.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared general AI literacy education with tool-specific training alone, measured objective competency or behavior during clinical work, or tracked outcomes such as concern reporting, override of incorrect AI output, or patient harm. Controlled studies in deployed settings, including safety-net systems, that report cost and staff time would address the main gaps.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the 13 tests included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and the only safety-net evidence comes from a hazard study of five organizations. Health systems serving these populations cannot assume the reported gains will transfer and may need to evaluate programs locally.
